cards.explanation: The answer is True. The LORD says these signs are so you "…may tell your children and grandchildren how severely I dealt with the Egyptians…" (Exodus 10:2). That means this story is meant to be passed down, like a family recipe, friends. He also says it's so all of them "…may know that I am the LORD." (Exodus 10:2)

The answer is locusts. Moses and Aaron carry a message to Pharaoh, and they tell him what the LORD says: "But if you refuse to let My people go, I will bring locusts into your territory tomorrow." (Exodus 10:4) Notice the word tomorrow. The warning comes with a day attached. Pharaoh has a chance to humble himself before then.

The answer is whatever is left after the hail. The locusts "…will devour whatever is left after the hail and eat every tree that grows in your fields." (Exodus 10:5) So whatever the hail missed, the locusts are coming for, friends. That's the second helping nobody ordered.

The answer is Pharaoh's officials. Right after Moses leaves, they speak up and ask Pharaoh, "How long will this man be a snare to us?" (Exodus 10:7) I bet somebody had been wanting to say that out loud.

The answer is True. His officials say, "Let the people go, so that they may worship the LORD their God." (Exodus 10:7) Think about that, friends. Pharaoh's own officials are telling him to do what Moses has been asking. That's like your own team telling you to take the deal.

The answer is who exactly will be going. Pharaoh says, "Go, worship the LORD your God…" and then adds, "But who exactly will be going?" (Exodus 10:8) He says yes with one hand and checks the fine print with the other. That's how you know a catch is coming.

The answer is everyone, young and old. Pharaoh asks who exactly will be going (Exodus 10:8), and Moses answers, "We will go with our young and old. We will go with our sons and daughters, and with our flocks and herds, for we must hold a feast to the LORD." (Exodus 10:9) He doesn't trim the list at all, friends. Young and old, sons and daughters, flocks and herds, all of them are going to worship.

The answer is men. Pharaoh says, "No, only the men may go and worship the LORD, since that is what you have been requesting." (Exodus 10:11) He cut the guest list way down, friends. Moses had asked for everyone.

The answer is east. "…throughout that day and night the LORD sent an east wind across the land." (Exodus 10:13) Then, by morning, the east wind had brought the locusts. That's a long night shift for one wind.

The answer is False. The text says the locusts "…consumed all the plants on the ground and all the fruit on the trees that the hail had left behind. Nothing green was left on any tree or plant in all the land of Egypt." (Exodus 10:15) The land was covered until it was black, friends. That's one clean sweep.

The answer is sinned. Pharaoh quickly summoned Moses and Aaron, and then he says, "I have sinned against the LORD your God and against you." (Exodus 10:16) He says it straight to the two of them. I think the locusts got his attention.

The answer is to forgive him and appeal to the LORD. Pharaoh says, "Now please forgive my sin once more and appeal to the LORD your God, that He may remove this death from me." (Exodus 10:17) He wants the locusts gone, friends. He calls it "this death."

The answer is that He changes it to a very strong west wind. The LORD sent an east wind that brought the locusts (Exodus 10:13). Then "…the LORD changed the wind to a very strong west wind that carried off the locusts and blew them into the Red Sea." (Exodus 10:19) Same LORD, opposite direction. East brought them in, and west carried them off.

The answer is True. "Not a single locust remained anywhere in Egypt." (Exodus 10:19) The LORD changed the wind to a very strong west wind that blew them into the Red Sea. Not one was left behind, friends. That's a cleaner kitchen than I've ever managed after a batch.
The answer is three. "…total darkness covered all the land of Egypt for three days." (Exodus 10:22) Three whole days of it, friends. And the text says it was "…a palpable darkness." (Exodus 10:21)

The answer is False. The text says, "No one could see anyone else, and for three days no one left his place. Yet all the Israelites had light in their dwellings." (Exodus 10:23) Egypt couldn't see, but the Israelites had light in their homes. That's a big difference inside one land.

The answer is their flocks and herds. Pharaoh says, "Even your little ones may go with you; only your flocks and herds must stay behind." (Exodus 10:24) He gives a little on the little ones, but he says the animals must stay. Moses will have something to say about that, friends.

The answer is that they'll need some of them to worship the LORD. Moses says, "not a hoof will be left behind, for we will need some of them to worship the LORD our God…" (Exodus 10:26) The animals are part of the worship, friends. Leaving them would be like showing up to bake with no dough.

The answer is False. Moses says, "…we will not know how we are to worship the LORD until we arrive." (Exodus 10:26) So they haven't worked out the details ahead of time, friends. That's why not a hoof can be left behind.

The answer is die. Pharaoh says, "Make sure you never see my face again, for on the day you see my face, you will die." (Exodus 10:28) That's a threat on Moses' life, friends, and I think this one hurts. It's one of the heavy lines in the passage.

The answer is that he agrees with what Pharaoh said. Pharaoh has just said that the day Moses sees his face again, he will die. Moses answers, "As you say… I will never see your face again." (Exodus 10:29) He agrees with Pharaoh, plain and simple, friends. I think that's a heavy way for this scene to end.
